description: Immortals , no matter time passes by we’re here working together one hand to make our vision come true
summary:
Humanity has sent many spacecraft to the Moon, Mars and deep space. Several made major discoveries, yet most people know them only as a name in a textbook or a small photo. Official mission pages are accurate but technical, so students and casual space fans rarely learn why these machines mattered, and the ones that went silent are easily forgotten.

Our solution is "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," an interactive website where each machine tells its own story. We built 13 animated 3D characters (3 on the Moon, 6 on Mars and 4 in deep space), each modeled on its real hardware so visitors see its true shape instead of a flat photo. Surveyor 3 is the host and introduces the others. When a visitor selects a machine, it speaks in the first person, in its own voice, like a friend: who it is, why it was built, when it launched, what it discovered and what condition it is in today. A side panel adds the science, pictures, a timeline and extra facts.

The impact is that space history becomes something visitors experience, not just read. Young learners and casual enthusiasts understand each mission faster, remember it longer and see how these machines helped us learn about other worlds. Every machine's legacy and current status stays visible, so none is forgotten.

The project meets the challenge by explaining what each artifact is, why it was sent, what it discovered and its current status, through a story-driven experience for school-age and casual audiences.
details:
"Abandoned, Not Forgotten" is an interactive 3D web experience that brings the machines humanity left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space back to life. Instead of reading a technical fact sheet, visitors explore a real-looking globe, meet each machine as an animated 3D character, and hear it tell its own story in the first person, like a friend. It is built for school-age learners and casual space fans.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Visitors choose a world (Moon, Mars or Deep Space) and explore it on an interactive globe with a timeline of missions. Selecting a landing site or machine opens an information panel and a character card. The machine introduces itself and tells its story in a fixed order: who it is, why it was built, when it launched, what it achieved, what we learned from it, and what condition it is in today. The narration is spoken aloud, and the text highlights in sync. The host character, Surveyor 3, welcomes visitors and comments on other machines along the way.

Each panel has five tabs: Story, Purpose and Science, Pictures, Facts and Timeline, and More. Every machine has its own 3D model built from its real hardware, so visitors see its true shape rather than a flat photo.

HOW TO USE IT

1. Open the website and choose "Turn on audio" or "Stay silent." Click Surveyor 3 to hear the introduction.

2. Choose a world from the top-left buttons: Moon, Mars or Deep Space.

3. Use the timeline buttons and arrows to move through the missions in order (for example, Moon: 1966-68, 1969, 1969-71, 1971-72, Now). On Mars, press Resume to play the tour automatically.

4. Click a site on the globe, or open Index to jump straight to any machine. Free Orbit lets you rotate and explore the surface freely.

5. Press Play Story to hear the machine speak. Use Pause and Replay as needed, and press Continue on the character card to move on.

6. Switch tabs for the science, pictures, key dates and extra facts. The NASA Data button shows the sources behind the content.

7. Press ESC or the close button to leave a panel. The speaker icon at the top right mutes everything.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Space history becomes something visitors experience, not just read. Learners understand each mission faster, remember it longer and see how these machines helped us learn about other worlds. Every machine's current status is shown, so silent spacecraft stay visible instead of being forgotten.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

React 19 and TypeScript for the app, three.js with @react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei for the 3D globe and characters, Tailwind CSS 4 and motion for design and animation, and the Web Audio API with edge-tts for narration. Development used GitHub, and the site is hosted on Cloudflare Workers.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Each machine narrates its own story in its own voice. Every character looks different and is based on its real hardware. A host character connects the stories, and the globe, timeline and narration turn history into a guided journey.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: all mission data was checked against NASA and NSSDC sources, and the site is honest about each machine's role (for example, Columbia explains that it was the command module, not the lander). Age-appropriate, plain language. Accessibility: sound is optional, and every story is also readable as text. Smooth performance on phones and computers.

DATA AND CREDITS

Mission data and images come from NASA sources and are credited to NASA.
